questions.title: What is the difference between a functional and a quality requirement?
explanation: A functional requirement states behavior or capability the system must provide. A quality requirement constrains characteristics such as latency, availability, security, accessibility, or maintainability and needs a measurable operating condition and threshold.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: Why should a requirement identify its stakeholder and rationale?
explanation: The stakeholder identifies whose need is served, while rationale explains the outcome or constraint behind the request. Together they help teams resolve conflicts, evaluate alternatives, and avoid preserving a proposed solution after the underlying need changes.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How should ambiguous words such as fast or user-friendly be corrected?
explanation: Replace them with observable scenarios and measurable acceptance criteria: named users, workload, environment, percentile, threshold, and measurement window. Keep the business intent alongside the metric so optimization does not defeat the real need.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is requirements traceability used for?
explanation: Traceability links a requirement to its source, design decisions, implementation, tests, releases, and evidence. It supports impact analysis and coverage without requiring every artifact to become a heavyweight document.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: When is a prototype evidence rather than a specification?
explanation: A prototype is evidence about usability, feasibility, or risk under stated assumptions. Unless explicitly hardened and accepted as the implementation contract, it does not define production reliability, security, accessibility, data integrity, or edge behavior.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is the difference between an assumption and a constraint?
explanation: An assumption is believed true for planning and should be validated because it may fail. A constraint is a binding limit or obligation, such as regulation, platform, deadline, or compatibility; both should have owners and consequences recorded.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How should conflicting stakeholder requirements be resolved?
explanation: Expose the conflict with scenarios, evidence, costs, risks, and decision authority. Seek an option that preserves underlying outcomes, then record the chosen tradeoff, rejected alternatives, and conditions that would reopen the decision.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What makes an acceptance criterion independent from an implementation?
explanation: It describes externally observable behavior, inputs, conditions, and expected results without prescribing internal classes, frameworks, or algorithms unless those are genuine constraints. This leaves implementation freedom while supporting objective acceptance.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: Why should error and recovery scenarios be captured with the happy path?
explanation: Failures define user trust, data integrity, and operational load. Capturing validation, timeout, partial completion, retry, cancellation, authorization, and recovery behavior early prevents each layer from inventing incompatible handling.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is an architecture decision record?
explanation: An ADR records a significant decision, context, forces, chosen option, status, and consequences. It preserves why the system is shaped a certain way and can be superseded when assumptions change rather than silently rewritten.

questions.title: When should an architectural decision be reversible?
explanation: Prefer reversible choices when evidence is weak or change is likely, using interfaces, migrations, or staged rollout to keep options open. Irreversible choices need stronger analysis, validation, and explicit ownership because correction cost is high.

questions.title: How does separation of concerns improve change safety?
explanation: Each module owns a coherent reason to change and interacts through explicit contracts. A change then affects fewer concepts and tests, reducing accidental coupling and making ownership and review more focused.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is the difference between logical and physical architecture?
explanation: Logical architecture describes responsibilities, boundaries, data flow, and contracts independent of deployment. Physical architecture maps those elements to processes, hosts, regions, networks, storage, and operational failure domains.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: Why should system boundaries be explicit?
explanation: Boundaries define trust, ownership, consistency, latency, failure propagation, and change contracts. Explicit boundaries make dependencies visible and let teams decide validation, authentication, retries, versioning, and observability at each crossing.

questions.title: How should a build-versus-buy decision be evaluated?
explanation: Compare total lifecycle cost, differentiation, integration, security, compliance, availability, data portability, vendor viability, exit cost, and internal capability. Validate critical claims with a bounded proof and record conditions that would change the choice.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What makes an interface contract stable?
explanation: A stable contract defines inputs, outputs, invariants, errors, ordering, idempotency, compatibility, and lifecycle without exposing unnecessary implementation details. Consumers can then evolve independently within the documented guarantees.

questions.title: Why should illegal states be difficult to represent?
explanation: Types, constructors, schemas, and state machines can encode invariants once instead of relying on scattered checks. This reduces invalid combinations and lets failures occur at a narrow trusted boundary.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is defensive programming at a trust boundary?
explanation: Validate untrusted inputs, enforce limits, fail with safe errors, and avoid assumptions about ordering, uniqueness, encoding, or caller behavior. Inside a well-defined trusted module, redundant checks may be replaced by enforced invariants.

questions.title: How does fail-fast differ from graceful degradation?
explanation: Fail-fast rejects invalid state early so corruption does not spread. Graceful degradation preserves a reduced but safe service when an optional dependency or capability fails; critical integrity and security checks should not degrade silently.

questions.title: What maintainability problem does this boolean-parameter call create?
explanation: The call site does not reveal what either boolean means and may permit confusing or invalid combinations. Named options, enums, or separate operations make intent visible and can encode valid states, though simple universally understood booleans may remain appropriate.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is temporal coupling in an API?
explanation: Temporal coupling requires operations in a hidden order, such as configure before start or read before close. Encode the sequence with construction, scoped resources, state-specific types, or an explicit protocol and make violations observable.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: When does a refactoring differ from a feature change?
explanation: Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving externally observable behavior; a feature change alters required behavior. Separating them when practical makes review, testing, rollback, and defect attribution easier.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: Why should comments explain intent rather than restate code?
explanation: The code already shows mechanics and can drift from duplicated prose. Durable comments capture non-obvious rationale, constraints, invariants, protocol details, or tradeoffs that a future maintainer cannot infer safely.

questions.title: What should happen when a function has too many responsibilities?
explanation: Identify distinct policies, effects, and data transformations, then extract cohesive operations with explicit inputs and outputs. Avoid fragmentation into trivial wrappers; the objective is understandable boundaries and independently testable decisions.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How can mutation at a distance create defects?
explanation: Shared mutable data can change through aliases that are invisible at the read site, breaking local reasoning and concurrency safety. Limit ownership, expose immutable values, and make state transitions explicit.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What does a small cohesive commit provide?
explanation: It represents one understandable change with tests and rationale, making review, bisecting, reverting, and cherry-picking safer. Small does not mean incomplete: the commit should preserve build and migration expectations.

questions.title: Why should generated files and source files not be mixed casually in review?
explanation: Large generated diffs hide meaningful source changes and are hard to review manually. Make generation reproducible, separate or clearly label generated artifacts, and verify that CI detects drift from the generator source.

questions.title: What is the purpose of semantic versioning?
explanation: Semantic versioning communicates compatibility intent through major, minor, and patch increments for a declared public API. It does not prove quality or eliminate migration work; the public contract and deprecation policy must still be defined.

questions.title: Why should dependency updates be reviewed like code changes?
explanation: An update changes executable behavior, transitive dependencies, licenses, vulnerabilities, platform support, and sometimes configuration. Review release notes and provenance, run relevant tests, and preserve a rollback path.

questions.title: How does trunk-based development reduce integration risk?
explanation: Frequent small integrations shorten divergence and surface conflicts and test failures early. Incomplete behavior is kept safe with branch-by-abstraction or controlled flags rather than long-lived branches.

questions.title: How do unit, integration, and end-to-end tests differ?
explanation: Unit tests isolate small logic quickly, integration tests verify boundaries and real collaborations, and end-to-end tests exercise deployed user workflows. A balanced strategy uses each where its failure signal and realism are most valuable.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What makes a test deterministic?
explanation: Given controlled inputs and environment, it produces the same result independent of run order, wall clock, network variability, random seed, or shared leftovers. Inject or control those sources and report enough context to reproduce failures.

questions.title: Why is retrying a flaky test not a complete fix?
explanation: Retries can reduce immediate noise while hiding races, pollution, unreliable dependencies, or invalid timing assumptions. Quarantine only with ownership and a deadline, preserve failure evidence, and remove the underlying nondeterminism.

questions.title: What is property-based testing useful for?
explanation: It generates many inputs to verify invariants such as round trips, ordering, conservation, or idempotency and shrinks failures to simpler cases. It complements carefully selected examples and model-based tests.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How does fuzz testing differ from property-based testing?
explanation: Fuzzing emphasizes large volumes of malformed or unexpected input to find crashes, hangs, and security failures. Property-based testing generates structured values to challenge declared invariants and typically offers domain-aware shrinking.

questions.title: Why should test fixtures be minimal?
explanation: Minimal fixtures make the behavior under test visible, reduce accidental coupling to unrelated defaults, and improve failure diagnosis. Reusable builders can provide valid baselines while each test overrides only meaningful fields.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is contract testing at a service boundary?
explanation: Contract tests verify that provider and consumer assumptions about requests, responses, errors, and compatibility agree without requiring every service in one environment. They supplement, rather than replace, deployed integration and resilience tests.

questions.title: Why can mocks make a test pass while production integration fails?
explanation: A mock can encode the test author's assumption rather than the real protocol, serialization, timing, or failure behavior. Use fakes, contract tests, containers, or real test instances for critical boundaries and keep mocks narrow.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What should a regression test prove after a defect?
explanation: It should fail for the demonstrated cause before the fix and pass afterward at the lowest boundary that reproduces the contract. Include relevant edge conditions and avoid merely asserting the implementation chosen for the fix.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How is branch coverage different from behavioral confidence?
explanation: Branch coverage reports which syntactic outcomes executed, not whether assertions were meaningful, requirements were complete, or important input combinations were tested. Use it to find gaps, not as a standalone quality target.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: When is mutation testing valuable?
explanation: Mutation testing changes program behavior systematically and checks whether tests fail, revealing assertions that execute code without distinguishing correct results. Apply it to important logic where the additional runtime and review cost is justified.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What does test isolation require for a database test?
explanation: Each test needs known schema and data, independent identifiers, controlled transactions or cleanup, and no reliance on execution order. Parallel tests require separate databases, schemas, or collision-safe records according to the engine's semantics.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: Why should a test assert observable outcomes instead of private methods?
explanation: Observable assertions preserve refactoring freedom and verify the contract users or collaborators depend on. Tests bound to private structure fail when implementation improves without behavior changing.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: How should time be controlled in automated tests?
explanation: Inject a clock or scheduler, use explicit time zones and instants, and advance virtual time where supported. Avoid sleeps and wall-clock assumptions that make tests slow and sensitive to daylight saving, leap behavior, or machine load.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is the testing value of a production-like environment?
explanation: It reveals database, network, identity, topology, resource, and deployment behavior absent from isolated tests. It still needs representative data and load; visual similarity or matching version numbers alone do not make it production-like.

questions.title: Why is average latency insufficient for a user-facing service?
explanation: An average hides the slow tail and traffic classes, so many users can suffer while the mean looks healthy. Measure percentile distributions segmented by operation, region, payload, and outcome with enough volume for interpretation.

questions.title: What is the difference between throughput and latency?
explanation: Throughput is work completed per unit time; latency is time for one operation. A system can increase throughput through batching while increasing individual latency, so targets must reflect the workload and user outcome.

questions.title: How should a performance bottleneck be identified?
explanation: Measure end-to-end latency under representative load, break it into queue, CPU, I/O, lock, network, and dependency time, then change one constrained resource or algorithm and remeasure. Optimize the dominant limiting path, not the most visible code.

questions.title: Why can adding concurrency reduce throughput?
explanation: Beyond a resource's capacity, more concurrent work increases queueing, context switching, lock contention, cache misses, and downstream pressure. Bound concurrency from measured service time and capacity, then apply backpressure.

questions.title: What is backpressure?
explanation: Backpressure lets a slower consumer limit or signal upstream production so queues and memory remain bounded. Systems may block, reject, shed, sample, or degrade work according to priority and correctness requirements.

questions.title: How should a load test be made representative?
explanation: Model real operation mix, payloads, data cardinality, concurrency, arrival patterns, cache state, dependencies, geography, and duration. Include warm-up and steady state, observe saturation and errors, and avoid generating load from the system under test.

questions.title: What is coordinated omission in latency measurement?
explanation: A load generator that waits for each slow response before sending more work under-samples requests that would have arrived during the stall. Measure against intended arrival time or use an open workload model to expose queueing delays.

questions.title: Why should capacity planning include headroom?
explanation: Headroom absorbs traffic variance, failover, deployments, dependency slowdown, and forecast error. Size it from risk and recovery time, monitor the leading constraint, and define when and how capacity will be added.

source.title: Google SRE: Software Engineering in SRE

questions.title: What is the difference between availability and reliability?
explanation: Availability measures whether service is usable over a period or fraction of requests. Reliability is broader predictable correctness over time, including integrity, latency, and failure-free operation; a service can be reachable yet wrong.

questions.title: How is an SLI different from an SLO?
explanation: An SLI is a measured indicator of user-visible service behavior, such as successful requests or latency. An SLO is the target for that indicator over a window; the remaining tolerated miss is the error budget.

questions.title: Why should an SLO be based on user journeys rather than server uptime alone?
explanation: Users care whether intended operations succeed within acceptable time. A process can be running while dependencies, data, or a subset of regions fail, so journey-based indicators better guide reliability decisions.

questions.title: What does an error budget help a team decide?
explanation: It quantifies tolerated unreliability and creates a shared basis for balancing release velocity with stability work. A documented policy can slow risky change when budget burn exceeds agreed thresholds.

questions.title: How should retries be budgeted?
explanation: Retry only transient, safe operations within the caller deadline; cap attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter, and account for each retry in downstream load. A retry budget prevents widespread failures from multiplying traffic indefinitely.

source.title: Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, Retries, and Backoff

questions.title: When is an operation idempotent?
explanation: Repeating it with the same intent produces the same intended effect, even if responses differ. Durable idempotency keys and atomic result recording make retried creation or payment operations safe across timeouts and duplicate delivery.

questions.title: Why can a circuit breaker make an outage worse if misconfigured?
explanation: Thresholds that are too sensitive can open during normal variance, synchronized recovery can cause a thundering herd, and fallback may overload another dependency. Tune from measured behavior, use jittered probes, and preserve observability.

questions.title: What is threat modeling intended to produce?
explanation: Threat modeling identifies assets, trust boundaries, attackers, abuse paths, and mitigations early enough to change design. Its output should drive requirements, tests, monitoring, and ownership rather than remain a one-time diagram.

questions.title: How does authentication differ from authorization?
explanation: Authentication establishes an identity or credential context. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a specific resource, and must be enforced at the trusted server boundary.

questions.title: What does least privilege require from a service account?
explanation: Grant only the operations, resources, environment, and duration required for its workload. Separate duties, rotate credentials, audit use, and test that forbidden operations fail rather than trusting an intended role name.

questions.title: Why is input validation not sufficient to prevent injection?
explanation: Validation constrains business input but cannot reliably escape every interpreter context. Keep data separate from commands using parameterized APIs, safe encoders, structured builders, and allow-listed identifiers.

questions.title: Where should output encoding occur?
explanation: Encode at the final output context because HTML text, attributes, URLs, CSS, JavaScript, shells, and SQL have different rules. Early generic escaping can be decoded, double-encoded, or applied to the wrong interpreter.

source.title: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

questions.title: How should secrets be handled throughout their lifecycle?
explanation: Generate with sufficient entropy, store in an access-controlled secret manager, distribute to the minimum workload, avoid logs and source control, rotate and revoke, audit access, and design recovery for compromise.

questions.title: Why is encryption at rest not a complete data-protection strategy?
explanation: Applications still decrypt data for use, and authorized identities, logs, backups, exports, and compromised runtime paths may expose it. Minimize collection, restrict access, separate keys, encrypt transport, audit use, and define retention and deletion.

questions.title: What is the difference between hashing and encryption?
explanation: Encryption is reversible with a key and protects confidentiality. Cryptographic hashing is one-way and supports integrity or password verification when used with an appropriate salted password-hashing scheme; the primitives are not interchangeable.

questions.title: How should security logging avoid creating another vulnerability?
explanation: Record actionable authentication, authorization, validation, and administrative events with time and correlation, but redact secrets and sensitive payloads, prevent log injection, protect transport and storage, and define access and retention.

questions.title: What is a software bill of materials used for?
explanation: An SBOM inventories software components and relationships so teams can assess exposure, licensing, provenance, and incident impact. It must be generated from trustworthy build inputs, retained per artifact, and connected to remediation workflows.

questions.title: Why should a build artifact have provenance?
explanation: Provenance records what source, dependencies, build process, and environment produced an artifact. Verifiable attestations help detect substitution and support incident analysis, but depend on protecting identities and build infrastructure.

questions.title: How should a vulnerability be prioritized?
explanation: Combine exploitability, exposure, affected assets, privileges, data impact, active exploitation, compensating controls, and remediation risk. A severity score is an input, not the queue by itself; assign an owner and deadline based on actual context.

questions.title: What is secure failure?
explanation: When a component cannot determine a safe outcome, it denies or contains the operation without revealing sensitive detail or leaving partial privileged state. Availability fallbacks must never silently bypass authorization or integrity controls.

questions.title: Why should dependency allow-lists and lockfiles both be used?
explanation: An allow-list controls which packages and sources are acceptable; a lockfile pins the resolved graph for repeatability. Neither validates maintainer trust or artifact integrity alone, so add scanning, signatures or provenance, review, and controlled updates.

questions.title: What does defense in depth mean without duplicating every control?
explanation: Use independent controls at meaningful trust boundaries so one failure does not expose the asset: identity, authorization, validation, isolation, encryption, monitoring, and recovery. Each layer needs a distinct failure mode and verified responsibility.

questions.title: What are the three main observability signals?
explanation: Metrics summarize numerical behavior over time, logs record discrete contextual events, and traces connect operations across a request path. Their schemas and correlation should be designed together around service questions and user outcomes.

questions.title: Why is high-cardinality telemetry expensive?
explanation: Dimensions such as user IDs, raw URLs, or request IDs create vast numbers of time series or index entries, increasing cost and query latency. Keep metric labels bounded and put unique correlation values in traces or controlled logs.

questions.title: What makes an alert actionable?
explanation: It indicates meaningful user or SLO impact, identifies the owning service, provides enough context and a runbook, and has a response expectation. Alerts for symptoms are usually more durable than alerts for every possible internal cause.

questions.title: Why should a runbook include verification and rollback?
explanation: Operators need to know whether each action improved the condition and how to return to a safe state if it did not. Include prerequisites, commands or controls, expected evidence, escalation, and ownership, and rehearse the procedure.

questions.title: What roles help coordinate a major incident?
explanation: Separate incident command, operations, communication, and planning or investigation responsibilities so one person is not overloaded and decisions are recorded. Adapt roles to incident size while maintaining a clear commander and handoffs.

questions.title: What makes a postmortem blameless but accountable?
explanation: It examines system conditions, incentives, information, and safeguards rather than punishing the person nearest the failure. Concrete corrective actions still have owners, priorities, evidence, and completion tracking.

questions.title: How should an incident timeline be constructed?
explanation: Normalize timestamps and gather alerts, deployments, logs, traces, tickets, and human decisions; distinguish observed facts from inference, identify detection and mitigation milestones, and record uncertainty. The timeline should support causal analysis, not assign blame.

questions.title: Why should a deployment be observable as its own event?
explanation: Version, configuration, flag, schema, and infrastructure changes provide context for shifts in errors, latency, and resource use. Emit deployment markers and correlate them with service telemetry so regressions are identified quickly.

questions.title: How do blue-green and canary deployments differ?
explanation: Blue-green switches traffic between complete old and new environments for fast rollback. A canary sends a small, controlled fraction to the new version and expands based on evidence, reducing blast radius but requiring representative traffic and analysis.

questions.title: What should gate a progressive rollout?
explanation: Use automatic and human gates based on error rate, latency, saturation, correctness, business outcomes, and guardrail metrics compared with a control. Define minimum sample, observation window, abort threshold, and rollback mechanics before starting.

questions.title: Why must database changes be backward compatible during rolling deployment?
explanation: Old and new application instances run concurrently and may read or write the same schema. Expand first, migrate and backfill safely, switch behavior, then contract only after old versions and data paths are gone.

source.title: AWS Builders' Library: Ensuring Rollback Safety

questions.title: How should configuration changes be released?
explanation: Version, review, validate, stage, and observe configuration with the same discipline as code. Detect incompatible combinations, protect secrets, record who changed what, and provide a tested rollback or safe default.

questions.title: What is the difference between rollback and roll-forward?
explanation: Rollback restores a known prior version and is fastest when changes are reversible and compatible. Roll-forward deploys a corrective change when data or interfaces cannot safely revert; both paths need rehearsal and time bounds.

questions.title: Why should disaster recovery be tested rather than documented only?
explanation: Backups may be incomplete, credentials unavailable, dependencies undocumented, or recovery too slow. Exercises verify restore integrity, recovery-point and recovery-time objectives, communication, permissions, and runbook accuracy.

questions.title: What should a backup restore test verify?
explanation: Restore into an isolated environment, validate schema and data integrity, required keys and dependencies, application startup, representative reads and writes, recovery time, and audit evidence. A successful backup job alone does not prove recoverability.

questions.title: How should engineering work be estimated under uncertainty?
explanation: Express assumptions, ranges, confidence, dependencies, and unknowns rather than a false precise date. Break discovery from delivery, update the forecast with evidence, and distinguish effort from elapsed time and commitment.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What is the difference between lead time and cycle time?
explanation: Lead time measures from request to delivery, while cycle time measures from active work start to completion. Queueing and prioritization can make lead time much larger, so both are needed to understand flow.

source.title: Google Cloud DevOps Research and Assessment

questions.title: Why is work in progress a system constraint?
explanation: Too much concurrent work increases queues, context switching, aging, integration risk, and time to feedback. Limiting work in progress exposes bottlenecks and helps teams finish valuable changes before starting more.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge

questions.title: What should a design review decide?
explanation: Confirm requirements and constraints, examine alternatives and risks, test failure and migration paths, identify security and operational implications, and assign unresolved questions. The output is a recorded decision and actions, not merely approval of a diagram.

questions.title: How can a team avoid knowledge silos?
explanation: Use shared reviews, pairing, rotations, documented decisions, tested runbooks, ownership backups, and deliberate onboarding. Measure whether another engineer can safely change and operate the area, not the amount of documentation produced.

questions.title: What makes documentation trustworthy?
explanation: It has a defined audience and owner, lives near the source of truth, states scope and version, is reviewed with changes, and is tested or generated where possible. Stale documentation should be discoverable and retired rather than silently retained.

questions.title: Why should a metric not become the goal by itself?
explanation: Teams optimize what is rewarded, sometimes reducing the real outcome while improving the number. Pair metrics with purpose, guardrails, qualitative evidence, and periodic review for gaming and unintended consequences.

questions.title: How should a risky technical experiment be structured?
explanation: State the hypothesis and success or stop criteria, bound time and blast radius, establish a baseline, change one major variable, capture evidence, and record a decision. Prototype artifacts should not enter production without the missing quality work.

questions.title: What is the purpose of a premortem?
explanation: Assume the project or launch failed and ask participants to describe plausible causes. The exercise surfaces risks that optimism or hierarchy suppresses, then converts the most credible causes into mitigations, signals, owners, and contingency plans.

questions.title: What evidence supports calling a software change complete?
explanation: Show accepted behavior and negative cases, security and accessibility checks, migration and rollback, production-like performance and reliability evidence, observability and ownership, documentation, deployment status, and any explicitly accepted residual risk. A green build alone proves only its configured checks passed.

source.title: Guide to the Software Engineering Body of Knowledge
